title: LIHTC 101
blurb: What the tax credit is, who it's for, how long it lasts, and the money that makes it work.

lessons.title: What LIHTC is
lessons.body:
The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, or LIHTC, is a federal tax credit created by the Tax Reform Act of 1986. It lives in Section 42 of the tax code, which is why you'll hear people call these "Section 42 properties."

Every year, each state gets a budget of credits based on its population. The state's housing finance agency hands them out to apartment projects through a competition, using a scoring plan called the Qualified Allocation Plan (QAP).

The developer who wins doesn't keep the credits. An investor, usually a bank, puts cash into the project in exchange for them. That cash is equity. It means the building needs less debt, and less debt is what lets the rents stay low.

Example, made-up numbers: a project receives $1,000,000 of credits a year for 10 years, or $10 million total. If an investor pays 83 cents per dollar of credit, that's $8.3 million of equity for the building.
Key points
  • A federal tax credit, Section 42 of the tax code.
  • States award it through a competition.
  • Investors buy the credits; the cash builds the apartments.
  • Less debt means lower rents.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42.
IRS, Low-Income Housing Credit overview.
lessons.more:
Where the credits come from

Congress sets the formula and the IRS adjusts it for inflation each year. For 2027, each state gets the greater of $3.53 per resident or $4,082,400. That pot covers the competitive 9% credits. The 4% credits work differently: they aren't capped by that formula, but they need tax-exempt bonds, and bonds are capped by a separate limit. See your state's credit budget and the bond cap.

Why a tax credit instead of a grant

The government could just write checks to build apartments. The tax credit does something different: it brings in private investors whose money is at risk for 15 years. If the property is badly run or breaks the rules, the investor can lose credits. That gives the investor a reason to watch the deal closely, which is a big part of why the program has lasted since 1986.

It also means the property is privately owned and privately managed. The government sets the rules and checks compliance, but it doesn't run the building.

How big it is

Since 1986, the program has helped finance about 4 million affordable homes, built or preserved. It's the largest source of funding for new affordable rental housing in the country.

Who's involved

  • The state housing finance agency writes the rules and awards the credits. See what QAPs reward.
  • The developer finds the site, applies, builds and usually stays on as the general partner. See the deal team.
  • The investor buys the credits, usually through a syndicator. See who owns the deal.
  • The residents have to income-qualify. See who can live there.

Common questions

Is it a tax break for the developer? Not really. The developer sells the credits. The tax benefit goes to the investor, and the cash goes into the building.

Do residents get a tax credit? No. Residents get a lower, capped rent.

Is it the same as Section 8? No. Section 8 vouchers help a renter pay rent. The tax credit helps pay to build the apartment. A renter can use a voucher at a tax credit property, though. See the voucher rule.

lessons.title: It's not public housing
lessons.body:
People mix these up all the time. Public housing is owned and run by a local housing authority, and residents usually pay about 30% of their own income in rent.

Most LIHTC properties are privately owned and privately managed. The rent is capped by the unit, based on the area's income limits, not by each resident's paycheck. A family earning less than the limit pays the same capped rent as a family right at the limit, unless they also have a voucher.

The two programs do overlap. When an old public housing site gets rebuilt, it's often financed with tax credits, and some units may keep deeper rental assistance. That's covered in the RAD lesson.

Key points
  • Public housing: owned by a housing authority; rent based on the resident's income.
  • LIHTC: usually private owners; rent capped by the unit's income limit.
  • They can be combined, especially in public housing rebuilds.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g) (rent restrictions).
HUD, Public Housing Program overview.
lessons.more:
Side by side

Public housingTax credit (LIHTC)Housing Choice Voucher
Who owns itLocal housing authorityUsually a private partnershipAny landlord who accepts it
What's subsidizedThe building and its operationsThe cost to buildThe renter's rent
How rent is setAbout 30% of the household's incomeCapped by the unit's income limitRenter pays about 30% of income; the voucher covers the rest, up to a limit
Who checks the rulesHUDThe state agency and the IRSThe housing authority

An example of how rent works

Example, made-up numbers: two families live in identical 60% AMI apartments where the capped rent is $1,050. One earns right at the limit; the other earns half that. Both pay $1,050. If the second family has a voucher, they pay about 30% of their income and the voucher pays the rest.

That's why tax credit housing alone isn't always affordable for the lowest-income families, and why many deals pair the credits with vouchers or other rental assistance.

One detail: when a family has a voucher, the voucher's share isn't counted toward the tax credit rent cap. So the total rent on a voucher unit can sometimes be higher than the cap, as long as the family's share stays within it.

Where they overlap

Many old public housing sites are being rebuilt with tax credits through RAD and Section 18. The housing authority often stays involved as a partner or landlord, and units can keep deep rental assistance. See the RAD lesson.

Common misconceptions

"It's government housing." Usually not. Most tax credit properties are privately owned and managed, and they often look like any other new apartment complex.

"Rent is based on what I make." Not in a tax credit unit, unless you also have a voucher or other rental assistance.

lessons.title: The 30-year promise
lessons.body:
A tax credit deal isn't a 10-year bet. There are three clocks:

  • Years 1–10: the credit period. Investors claim the credits a little at a time.
  • Years 1–15: the compliance period. Incomes get checked and rents stay capped. If the property breaks the rules, the IRS can take credits back.
  • Years 16–30+: extended use. At least 15 more years of affordability, recorded against the property and enforced by the state.

That's at least 30 years, and plenty of states ask for longer. California's agreements, for example, run 55 years. Ownership often changes hands around year 15, but the rent rules stay with the property. More on that in the Year 15 lesson.

Key points
  • 10 years of credits.
  • 15-year compliance period, enforced by the IRS.
  • At least 15 more years of extended use, enforced by the state.
  • Many states require longer.
sources: California Tax Credit Allocation Committee regulations (55-year term).
lessons.more:
The timeline

WhenWhat happensWho enforces it
Placed in serviceThe building is ready for residents; the clocks start
Years 1–10Investor claims credits each yearIRS
Years 1–15Compliance period: incomes checked, rents cappedState agency and IRS (credits can be recaptured)
Years 16–30+Extended use: rules still applyState agency, through the recorded agreement

Why there are two enforcers

During the first 15 years, breaking the rules can cost the investor credits, so the IRS has teeth. After year 15, there are no credits left to take back. The affordability rules keep going because they're written into a recorded agreement on the property, often called a LURA (land use restriction agreement). The state enforces that agreement, and it binds whoever owns the property.

Why many deals last longer than 30 years

Federal law requires states to favor projects that stay affordable the longest. So many states award points for longer commitments, or require them outright. California's agreements run 55 years.

What happens at the end

When the agreement finally ends, an owner may be able to move to market rents. In practice, many properties get rehabbed with new credits and a new agreement first, which resets the clock. Losing affordable units this way is a real concern for housing advocates, often called "expiring use."

Common questions

Can the rules end early? Rarely. One path, the qualified contract, is covered in the Year 15 lesson. Many states now require owners to give it up.

Do residents have to move at year 15? No. The rent rules continue through extended use.

lessons.title: Who can live there, and how rent is set
lessons.body:
Every deal picks one of three minimum set-asides:

  • 20/50: at least 20% of units for households earning 50% or less of area median income (AMI).
  • 40/60: at least 40% of units for households at 60% of AMI or less.
  • Income averaging: at least 40% of units, with income limits that average 60% of AMI or less and no unit above 80%. See the income averaging lesson.

In practice, most deals make nearly every unit affordable, because credits are only earned on the affordable units.

Rent is capped too. Gross rent, meaning rent plus a utility allowance, can't be more than 30% of the income limit for that unit. The limit is figured using 1.5 people per bedroom, so a two-bedroom is priced off a three-person household.

One rule surprises people: a household made up entirely of full-time students generally doesn't qualify, with some exceptions such as single parents and students who receive certain public assistance.

Example, made-up numbers: if the 60% AMI income limit for a three-person household is $48,000, the maximum gross rent for a two-bedroom at 60% is 30% × $48,000 ÷ 12 = $1,200 a month, including the utility allowance.
Key points
  • Three set-aside options: 20/50, 40/60, income averaging.
  • Gross rent capped at 30% of the unit's income limit.
  • Rent is priced off 1.5 people per bedroom.
  • All-student households generally don't qualify.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(1) (set-asides), § 42(g)(2) (rent limits, imputed household size), § 42(i)(3)(D) (students).
HUD, Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project (MTSP) income limits.
lessons.more:
Where income limits come from

HUD publishes income limits for tax credit properties every year, by county or metro area and by household size. They're called MTSP limits (Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project). The 50% and 60% limits are the ones most deals use. Pick yours below.

How rent is figured

Rent is tied to the size of the apartment, not who actually lives in it. The rule assumes 1.5 people per bedroom (one person for a studio):

UnitHousehold size used
Studio1 person
1 bedroom1.5 people
2 bedrooms3 people
3 bedrooms4.5 people

For half-person sizes, the limit is averaged between the two household sizes. Then: maximum gross rent = 30% of that income limit, divided by 12. Try it in the rent cap calculator.

What counts as income

Generally the same definition HUD uses for Section 8: wages, Social Security, pensions, child support, and income from assets above certain amounts, for everyone in the household. The property verifies it with documents before move-in, and the household signs a certification.

The student rule, in more detail

A household where everyone is a full-time student generally can't live in a tax credit unit. Exceptions include:

  • A student receiving TANF assistance.
  • A student in certain government job training programs.
  • Single parents and their children, if none are claimed as dependents by someone else.
  • Married students filing a joint return.
  • Students who were previously in foster care.

Common questions

Is there a minimum income? Federal law doesn't set one, but many properties use a rent-to-income screen. Rules on that vary, especially for voucher holders.

What if my household gets bigger or smaller? The unit's rent doesn't change with household size. Your eligibility is based on your actual household size at move-in. See what happens if you get a raise.

lessons.title: 9% vs 4% deals
lessons.body:
There are two flavors of credit. The names come from roughly how much of a building's eligible cost the credits are worth each year.

  • 9% credits are designed to be worth about 70% of eligible costs in present value. They're scarce, so states award them competitively through the QAP. The 9% rate is now a fixed minimum for new construction and rehab.
  • 4% credits are designed to be worth about 30%. They don't come out of the state's competitive budget. Instead, a project gets them automatically if enough of it is financed with tax-exempt private activity bonds. The 4% rate has been a fixed minimum since 2021.

The trade-off: 9% deals bring much more equity but are hard to win. 4% deals are easier to get but leave a bigger gap that soft money, a bigger loan or a deferred fee has to fill. Either way, credits are claimed over 10 years.

Key points
  • 9%: about 70% of costs in value, competitive.
  • 4%: about 30%, comes with tax-exempt bonds.
  • 4% deals need more money from other sources.
  • Both are claimed over 10 years.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(b) (applicable percentages and minimums), § 42(h)(4) (bond-financed buildings).
Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (4% minimum).
lessons.more:
Side by side

9% credits4% credits
Where they come fromThe state's annual credit budgetAutomatic with enough tax-exempt bond financing
How you get themWin a scored competition (the QAP)Get bond volume cap and meet the bond test
Minimum annual rate9% (new construction and rehab)4%
Rough valueAbout 70% of eligible costsAbout 30% of eligible costs
Bonds neededNoYes, at least 25% of building and land cost (for buildings placed in service after 2025 with some post-2025 bonds; 50% before)
Typical challengeWinning the awardFilling the bigger financing gap

Why the rates are "at least"

The rates used to float monthly, set by the Treasury to hit the 70% and 30% values. Congress later locked in minimums: 9% for new construction and substantial rehab that isn't federally subsidized, and 4% for buildings that received allocations, or were financed by bonds issued, after 2020. Buying an existing building earns the 4% rate. Today both work as fixed rates.

See the difference

Put the same building through the capital stack calculator and flip between 9% and 4%. The 4% version brings in much less equity, so the gap gets much bigger.

Example, made-up numbers: $17M of eligible basis. At 9%, that's $1.53M of credit a year; at 83 cents, about $12.7M of equity. At 4%, it's $680K a year, or about $5.6M of equity. Same building, $7M less.

So why would anyone do a 4% deal?

  • There's no annual competition to win, so it can move on the developer's timeline.
  • Bigger projects that would blow past a state's per-deal 9% limit can still work.
  • The bonds can carry an attractive loan, and some states pair 4% deals with their own soft money or state credits.

Some deals even combine the two on separate buildings, where the state allows it.

lessons.title: The capital stack
lessons.body:
No affordable deal is paid for by one source. It's a stack, and every piece comes with strings.

  • Tax credit equity. Usually the biggest piece. No monthly payment, but strict rules for decades.
  • A first mortgage. A regular loan. Rents are capped, so the loan has to stay small enough for the property to pay it.
  • Soft loans and grants. State, city or Federal Home Loan Bank money. Cheap or forgiven, but competitive and slow.
  • Deferred developer fee. The developer leaves part of their fee in the deal and gets paid later from cash flow. It closes the last gap.
Example, made-up numbers: a $20 million deal paid for with $13M of tax credit equity (65%), a $4M first mortgage (20%), $2M of soft money (10%) and a $1M deferred developer fee (5%).

Module 4, Paying for it, takes each piece apart.

Key points
  • Every deal is layered.
  • Equity is the biggest piece.
  • The mortgage is limited by capped rents.
  • Soft money and deferred fee fill the gap.
sources: Example numbers are made up for illustration.
lessons.more:
Sources must equal uses

Every deal has two columns. Uses is what it costs: land, construction, fees, reserves. See the development budget. Sources is where the money comes from. They have to match to the dollar before closing. Whatever the main sources don't cover is the gap.

The layers, top to bottom

  1. First mortgage. Gets paid first from the property's income. Sized by what capped rents can support. See why the mortgage is small.
  2. Soft loans. Get paid only from leftover cash flow, if any, and are often forgiven at the end. See soft money.
  3. Deferred developer fee. Paid from cash flow after the loans. See the developer fee.
  4. Tax credit equity. Not a loan at all. Investors are paid back in credits and tax losses, not cash.

Try it

The capital stack calculator lets you change costs, rents, interest rates and credit prices and watch the gap grow or shrink. Flip between 9% and 4% to see why 4% deals need so much more soft money.

How gaps get closed

  • Apply for more soft money (slow and competitive).
  • Defer more of the developer fee (only as much as cash flow can realistically pay back).
  • Cut costs through value engineering.
  • Get a basis boost if the site qualifies. See the basis boost.
  • Change the unit mix or the number of units.

If none of those works, the deal doesn't happen.

lessons.title: Why $1 of credit sells for about 83 cents
lessons.body:
Developers don't get a dollar for every dollar of credit. In the second quarter of 2026, investors paid about 82.7 cents on average, down from about 85 cents a year earlier.

Why the discount:

  • Investors wait. The credits come in over 10 years. A dollar in year 10 is worth less than a dollar today.
  • Investors take risk. If the property breaks the rules during the 15-year compliance period, the IRS can take credits back.
  • Investors want a return. Paying less than $1 now is how they earn one.

Some investors pay more. Banks get Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) credit for investing in certain markets, so pricing tends to be stronger where banks want CRA credit. And in 2026, more deals reached the market than investor money could absorb (a 2025 backlog, easier 4% deals and 12% more 9% credits), so prices slipped.

Key points
  • Pricing is cents per dollar of credit.
  • Time, risk and return explain the discount.
  • CRA demand pushes prices up in some markets.
  • About 83 cents in mid-2026.
sources: Affordable Housing Finance, 2026 midyear LIHTC investor survey (Q2 2026 average of 82.7 cents, down from 85.3; supply drivers and slower investor capital growth).
CohnReznick Tax Credit Monitor (Feb–May 2026 median of about $0.835).
26 U.S.C. § 42(f), § 42(j).
lessons.more:
How pricing is quoted

Pricing is stated as cents of equity per dollar of credit the investor will receive over 10 years. "83 cents" means the investor pays $0.83 now for each $1.00 of credit it will claim.

Example, made-up numbers: a deal gets $1.5M of credit a year, or $15M over 10 years. At 83 cents, that's $12.45M of equity. At 90 cents, it's $13.5M. That 7-cent difference is $1.05M, which can decide whether the deal works.

What moves the price

  • CRA demand: banks that want Community Reinvestment Act credit in a market compete for deals there.
  • Investors' tax appetite: credits only help investors with enough tax liability to use them.
  • Interest rates: higher rates make investors want a higher return, which lowers the price.
  • Supply: when deals grow faster than investor money, prices fall. That happened in 2026, with a 2025 backlog, easier 4% deals and 12% more 9% credits all hitting at once.
  • Deal risk: the sponsor's track record, the market and the structure all matter.

Who's buying

Most investors are banks and large companies. Many invest through syndicators, firms that pool investor money into funds and buy into many deals. Some large banks invest directly.

Why developers care so much

Price is one of the biggest numbers in the whole deal. Every cent of price on a $15M credit award is $150,000 of equity. Try changing the price in the capital stack calculator.

lessons.title: What changed in 2026
lessons.body:
The tax law signed July 4, 2025 (Public Law 119-21) made two big changes for affordable housing, both starting in 2026:

  • 12% more 9% credits, permanently. Each state's annual credit budget went up 12%. That's why the 2026 amount was $3.416 per resident.
  • An easier bond test. 4% deals used to need tax-exempt bonds covering 50% of the building and land cost. For buildings placed in service after 2025, it's 25%, as long as at least 5% of that cost is financed with bonds issued after 2025. That stretches each state's bond cap across more projects.

What didn't make it: a 30% basis boost for rural and tribal areas was in the House version but dropped from the final law.

The catch: deals grew faster than investor money, and pricing softened. See tax credit pricing.

Key points
  • Signed July 4, 2025.
  • 9% credits up 12%, permanently.
  • 4% bond test cut from 50% to 25%.
  • Rural and tribal basis boost was not included.
sources: Public Law 119-21 (2025).
IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 per-capita amount).
EY Tax News, July 10, 2025; Moss Adams, 2025 (rural boost dropped).
Nixon Peabody, "Low-income housing and community development tax credits in the Big Beautiful Bill" (July 16, 2025) (25% test details).
lessons.more:
What the 12% increase means in dollars

Without the change, the 2026 amount would have been $3.05 per resident. With it, it was $3.416.

Example, made-up numbers: a state with 5 million residents gets about $1.8M more annual credit authority in 2026 than it would have. At roughly $1.5M per award, that's about one more deal a year, every year.

What the 25% bond test means

To get 4% credits, a building used to need tax-exempt bonds covering at least 50% of its building and land cost. Now it's 25%, for buildings placed in service after 2025 that have at least 5% of that cost financed with bonds issued after 2025.

Example, made-up numbers: a project with $40M of building and land cost used to need $20M of bonds. Now it needs $10M. A state's bond cap can stretch across about twice as many deals of that size.

Bonds are still capped (see the bond cap), so the change matters most in states where bond cap was the bottleneck.

What didn't change

  • Credits are still claimed over 10 years.
  • The 15-year compliance period and extended use stayed the same.
  • Income limits and rent caps work the same way.
  • No new basis boost for rural or tribal areas.

Side effects to watch

Deals grew faster than investor money, which softened pricing. More 4% deals can compete for the same soft money and the same construction crews. The net effect should still be more homes, but the gap on each deal doesn't disappear.

title: Sizing the credit
blurb: How an award gets calculated, where the address adds 30%, and how much each state has to give out.

lessons.title: Three numbers, one award
lessons.body:
Every tax credit award comes from the same formula:

  • Eligible basis: what it cost to build the apartments. Land doesn't count.
  • Applicable fraction: the share of the building that's affordable, by units or by floor space, whichever is lower. If every unit is restricted, it's 100%.
  • Credit rate: at least 9% a year for a new 9% deal, at least 4% for a 4% deal.

Eligible basis × applicable fraction = qualified basis. Qualified basis × credit rate = the annual credit, claimed for 10 years.

Example, made-up numbers: $10M of eligible basis × 100% × 9% = $900,000 of credit a year, or $9 million over 10 years. The developer sells that to an investor for cash.

In practice, the state also checks the deal's funding gap and awards only what the deal needs, which can be less than the formula. More eligible basis still means more credit, which is why what counts as basis, and where you build, matter so much.

Key points
  • Eligible basis × applicable fraction × rate.
  • Land isn't in basis.
  • Claimed every year for 10 years.
  • States can award less than the formula if the deal needs less.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(m)(2) (credit limited to the amount needed for feasibility).
26 U.S.C. § 42(c)(1)(B)–(D) (unit and floor-space fractions), § 42(f)(2) (first-year credit and year 11), § 42(m)(2)(C) (three-point feasibility review).
lessons.more:
The formula, one step at a time

StepWhat it meansExample, made-up numbers
1. Eligible basisDepreciable cost of the building and related costs (land excluded)$12,000,000
2. Applicable fractionLower of the unit share and the floor-space share that's affordable72 of 80 units = 90%; 63,000 of 72,000 sq ft = 87.5%. Use 87.5%
3. Qualified basisStep 1 × step 2$12,000,000 × 87.5% = $10,500,000
4. Annual creditStep 3 × credit rate$10,500,000 × 9% = $945,000 a year
5. Total creditsAnnual credit × 10 years$9,450,000

Why the “lower of” rule matters

The applicable fraction uses whichever share is smaller, units or square feet. If the market-rate apartments are bigger than the affordable ones, the floor-space share drops and so does the credit. That's why most tax credit deals make every unit affordable: 100% is the simplest way to get the full credit.

The first year is usually partial

Credits start the year the building is placed in service, or the next year if the owner chooses. In the first year, the credit is based on how many apartments are actually leased to qualified households each month. Whatever is lost while the building fills up isn't gone: it's claimed in year 11. So the total stays the same, it just takes a little longer to collect.

The state checks the math three times

The credit agency has to award no more than the deal needs to be financially feasible. It reviews the sources and uses of funds when the application comes in, when credits are allocated, and when the building is placed in service. If costs come in lower, or other funding comes in higher, the final award can shrink.

Run your own numbers in the capital stack calculator.

lessons.title: The 30% basis boost
lessons.body:
Two identical buildings can get very different awards. The difference is the address.

In certain areas, the tax code lets a deal count 130% of its eligible basis (for an existing building, only the rehab costs get the boost, not the purchase price):

  • Qualified Census Tracts (QCTs): tracts where at least half of households earn under 60% of area median income, or the poverty rate is 25% or more.
  • Difficult Development Areas (DDAs): places where land, construction and utility costs are high compared to local incomes.
  • State-designated buildings: a state agency can give the boost to a 9% building that needs it to be financially feasible. This one isn't available to bond-financed 4% deals.
Example, made-up numbers: $10M of basis becomes $13M. At 9%, that's $1.17M of credit a year instead of $900K, about $2.7M more over 10 years.

HUD redraws the QCT and DDA maps every year. The 2027 lists were announced in October 2026. A boost for all rural and tribal areas was proposed in 2025 but didn't make it into law.

Key points
  • Count 130% of eligible basis.
  • QCTs: lower-income tracts.
  • DDAs: high-cost areas.
  • Or the state designates the building (9% only).
  • The map changes every year.
sources: HUD, 2027 Difficult Development Areas and Qualified Census Tracts (Federal Register, Oct. 6, 2026).
Rural basis boost omitted from P.L. 119-21: Housing Assistance Council; Moss Adams.
HUD QCT/DDA notices: 20% population limit, Small Area DDAs (since 2016), 730-day application rule in the 2027 notice, Docket FR-6565-N-02.
Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (state-designated boost, § 42(d)(5)(B)(v)).
lessons.more:
The boost in dollars

Example, made-up numbersNo boostWith the 30% boost
Eligible basis$12,000,000$15,600,000
Annual credit (100% affordable, 9%)$1,080,000$1,404,000
Credits over 10 years$10,800,000$14,040,000
Equity at 83 cents$8,964,000$11,653,200

Same building, same costs: about $2.7 million more equity. HUD designates an area as a QCT or a DDA, not both, and the boost is capped at 130% either way.

How the maps are drawn

  • QCTs are census tracts. HUD uses Census income and poverty data, and the tracts it picks can't hold more than 20% of a metro area's population.
  • DDAs compare costs to incomes, using HUD's Fair Market Rents and income limits. In metro areas, HUD has drawn DDAs by ZIP code since 2016 (called Small Area DDAs). Outside metro areas, it uses whole counties. DDAs also can't cover more than 20% of the population.

What if the map changes?

Because the lists change every year, HUD's notices include a grace period. If a complete application is filed while the site is on the list, and before the next year’s lists take effect, the deal generally keeps the boost as long as the credits are awarded (or, for a 4% deal, the bonds are issued or the building is placed in service) within 730 days of that application, under HUD’s 2027 notice. Check the exact rule in the current HUD notice for any real deal.

The state-designated boost

Since 2008, a state can give the boost to a 9% building outside a QCT or DDA if the state decides the building needs it to be financially feasible. Each state sets its own rules in its plan (the QAP). Some use it for rural deals, some for high-opportunity areas, and some barely use it. Bond-financed 4% deals can't use this route; they need a QCT or DDA.

Check an address

HUD publishes the QCT and DDA lists and an online map where you can look up any address. Start at HUD User's QCT and DDA page.

lessons.title: What counts in eligible basis
lessons.body:
Since credits are sized off eligible basis, every line in the budget gets a question: is it in basis or not?

Usually in: construction of the residential building, much of the site work tied to it, architecture and engineering, construction-period interest and fees, permits, and the developer fee (within the state's cap). Common areas like a community room or laundry count if residents aren't charged extra to use them.

Usually out: land, permanent loan costs, reserves, marketing, syndication costs, and commercial space.

Things that shrink it: federal grants used for the building reduce eligible basis. That's why many federal soft funds are made as loans instead.

Existing buildings: for a rehab deal, the cost of buying an existing building can count as acquisition basis at the 4% rate, generally if it was last placed in service (or last substantially improved) more than 10 years before the purchase, with some exceptions. The rehab work itself has to meet a minimum: the greater of 20% of the building's basis or a per-unit amount ($9,000 per low-income unit for 2027).

Key points
  • Building costs and most soft costs are in.
  • Land, reserves and permanent loan costs are out.
  • Federal grants reduce basis.
  • Acquisition basis can earn 4% credits on existing buildings.
sources: IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35 (2027 rehab per-unit minimum).
Item-by-item treatment varies; deals rely on tax counsel and a cost certification.
26 U.S.C. § 42(d)(5)(A) (federal grants), § 42(i)(2) (below-market federal loans, after HERA 2008), § 42(l)(1) (Form 8609).
lessons.more:
A budget, sorted

Budget line (made-up numbers)CostIn eligible basis?
Land$1,500,000No
Building construction and related site work$14,000,000Yes
Architecture and engineering$700,000Yes
Construction loan interest and fees$600,000Yes
Developer fee (within the state cap)$2,000,000Yes
Permanent loan fees$150,000No
Operating and replacement reserves$400,000No
Syndication and marketing$100,000No
Total$19,450,000$17,300,000 in basis

In this example, about 89% of the total cost is in eligible basis. The other $2,150,000 doesn't generate any credits, even though the deal still has to pay for it.

The gray areas

Site work is a common debate. Work that's tied to the building, like grading under it or utility connections, is usually in. Work that is really part of the land, or that would last no matter what's built, often isn't. The line is set by tax rules and case law, not by the budget's labels. That's why deals lean on tax counsel and an accountant's cost certification.

Grants versus loans

If a federal grant pays for part of the building, eligible basis drops by the grant amount. That means fewer credits. So many federal soft funds, like HOME, are usually structured as loans to the partnership, which don't reduce basis. Since 2008, below-market federal loans no longer force a building down to the 4% rate.

The check at the end

Once the building is placed in service, the owner gets a cost certification, an audit of what was actually spent and what's in basis. The state uses it to set the final credit amount and issue IRS Form 8609, which the owner needs to claim the credits.

lessons.title: From award to cash
lessons.body:
Here's what a $1 million award actually turns into.

Example, made-up numbers: $1,000,000 of credit a year × 10 years = $10,000,000 of total credits. At 83 cents per dollar, the investor pays about $8,300,000 into the partnership.

A few things to know about that $8.3M:

  • It doesn't arrive all at once. Investors pay in installments tied to milestones. See the pay-in lesson.
  • The investor gets the credits plus the property's tax losses, mostly depreciation. Both count toward its return.
  • If the credits come in late or short, the agreement usually cuts the investor's payments. Those are called adjusters.
Key points
  • Annual credit × 10 × price = equity.
  • Paid in installments, not one check.
  • Investors get credits and tax losses.
  • Shortfalls trigger adjusters.
sources: Example numbers and pricing are made up for illustration; actual pricing varies by deal and market.
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(1)(E) (carryover allocations: 10% test, placed-in-service deadline), § 42(l)(1) (Form 8609).
Pay-in percentages and adjuster amounts are made up; every partnership agreement negotiates its own.
lessons.more:
The path from award to cash

  1. Award. The state reserves credits for the deal.
  2. Carryover. Most 9% deals aren't built in the year they win. A carryover allocation holds the credits. To keep them, the owner generally has to spend more than 10% of the expected basis within 12 months, and place the building in service by the end of the second calendar year after the award.
  3. Closing. The developer closes with the investor and lenders and starts construction. The first equity installment comes in.
  4. Construction to lease-up. More installments arrive as milestones are hit.
  5. Form 8609. After the cost certification, the state issues Form 8609, and the last installment is usually paid.

A sample pay-in schedule

Milestone (made-up percentages)ShareAmount
Closing20%$1,660,000
Construction complete40%$3,320,000
Stabilized occupancy25%$2,075,000
Form 8609 received15%$1,245,000
Total100%$8,300,000

Every deal negotiates its own schedule. Because so much equity comes late, the construction loan usually covers the gap until it arrives.

How adjusters work

Example, made-up numbers: the deal was priced on $10,000,000 of credits, but the final cost certification supports only $9,500,000, 5% less. At 83 cents, the investor's total drops by $415,000, to $7,885,000. If the first-year credits come in later than promised, a timing adjuster can cut the price too.

Some agreements also have an upward adjuster if credits come in higher, usually with a cap. Either way, the price per credit is the number to watch: total equity ÷ total credits.

lessons.title: The nonprofit set-aside
lessons.body:
Federal law requires each state to reserve at least 10% of its credit budget for projects where a qualified nonprofit owns an interest and materially participates in development and operations.

A qualified nonprofit is a 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4) whose exempt purposes include fostering low-income housing. It can't be controlled by a for-profit.

Many states go further, with their own nonprofit or community-based pools. That's one reason you see for-profit developers partner with local nonprofits and housing authorities.

Key points
  • At least 10% of every state's credits.
  • The nonprofit must materially participate.
  • States can set aside more.
  • It's a big reason for nonprofit partnerships.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(5)(B)–(D) (90% limit, qualified nonprofit, subsidiaries), § 469(h) (material participation), § 42(i)(7) (right of first refusal).
lessons.more:
What counts as a qualified nonprofit

  • A 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(4) organization.
  • One of its exempt purposes includes fostering low-income housing.
  • The state agency determines it isn't affiliated with or controlled by a for-profit organization.
  • It owns an interest in the project, directly or through a wholly owned subsidiary.
  • It materially participates, meaning regular, continuous and substantial involvement in development and operations throughout the compliance period, not just a name on the paperwork.

Why it's at least 10%

The law says no more than 90% of a state's credit ceiling can go to projects outside the nonprofit set-aside. So the 10% is a floor, not a cap. Nonprofit-sponsored deals can also win credits in a state's other pools.

The year-15 connection

The tax code also lets a qualified nonprofit, tenant group or government agency hold a right of first refusal to buy the property after the 15-year compliance period, at a price that can be as low as the outstanding debt (not counting debt taken on in the last 5 years) plus the taxes the sale triggers. That can help keep the property affordable long term. Read more in the year-15 lesson.

What it means for partnerships

A for-profit developer can still be involved: it can partner with a qualified nonprofit that holds an ownership interest and is actively involved. States review these partnerships, and some QAPs ask for proof of the nonprofit's role, like board minutes or a development agreement.

lessons.title: Your state's 2027 credit budget
lessons.body:
Each state's annual 9% credit budget is set by a per-person formula, adjusted for inflation every year.

For 2027: the greater of $3.53 per resident or $4,082,400 for small states. That's up from $3.416 in 2026, the first year with the permanent 12% increase.

Example, made-up numbers: a state with 5 million residents gets about $17.65 million of annual credit authority. Since each award is claimed for 10 years, that's about $176.5 million of total credits handed out in one year.

On top of the per-person amount, states can re-award credits that were returned by earlier deals and may get a share of a small national pool of unused credits.

Two things to remember: the budget is in annual credits, and it's almost always oversubscribed. Most states get more requests than they can fund, often by a wide margin.

Key points
  • 2027: $3.53 per resident, or $4,082,400 minimum.
  • Budgets are in annual credits.
  • Returned credits get re-awarded.
  • Demand far exceeds supply.
sources: IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35 (2027 amounts); Novogradac, 2026.
IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32, as updated by the IRS for P.L. 119-21 (2026 amount of $3.416).
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(3)(C)–(D) (ceiling components, carryforward, national pool). Threshold: $4,082,400 ÷ $3.53 ≈ 1,156,000 residents.
lessons.more:
What's in a state's ceiling

The per-person amount is the biggest piece, but a state's total credit ceiling for a year adds up four parts:

  • The per-person amount (or the small-state minimum).
  • Credits left unused from the year before. A state gets one extra year to use them.
  • Credits returned by earlier deals that didn't use them.
  • A share of the national pool, unused credits collected from other states and split among states that used up their own.

Who gets the minimum

For 2027, the small-state minimum of $4,082,400 beats $3.53 per person in any state with fewer than about 1,156,000 residents. Bigger states get more in total, but the smallest states get more per person.

Where the budget goes

Each state's Qualified Allocation Plan (QAP) decides how to split it, often into set-asides for nonprofits, rural areas, seniors or supportive housing, with the rest competing statewide or by region. See what QAPs reward.

Pick your state

lessons.title: The cap behind every 4% deal
lessons.body:
4% deals don't use the state's credit budget, but they're still rationed. The bonds they need count against the state's private activity bond volume cap.

For 2027: each state's cap is the greater of $135 per resident or $410,520,000.

Housing isn't the only use. The same cap covers single-family mortgage revenue bonds, some industrial and student loan bonds, and other uses. The state decides how to split it, and in many states housing applications far exceed the cap.

That's why the 2026 change to a 25% bond test matters. A project that used to need bonds for half of its building-and-land basis now needs them for a quarter, so the same cap can support more deals.

Key points
  • 4% deals need volume-cap bonds.
  • 2027: $135 per resident, or $410.52M minimum.
  • Housing competes with other uses.
  • The 25% test stretches the cap further.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 146 (volume cap); § 42(h)(4).
IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-35 (2027 amounts).
Public Law 119-21 (25% test for buildings placed in service after 2025, with at least 5% of aggregate basis financed by post-2025 bonds).
26 U.S.C. § 146(f) (carryforward elections, 3 years). Example numbers made up.
lessons.more:
Why the 25% test stretches the cap

Made-up numbersOld 50% testNew 25% test
Building and land basis per deal$40,000,000$40,000,000
Bonds needed per deal$20,000,000$10,000,000
Deals $200,000,000 of housing cap can support1020

In practice, many deals still use more bonds than the minimum when the bonds carry a good loan. The new test applies to buildings placed in service after 2025 when bonds issued after 2025 finance at least 5% of the building-and-land basis.

How states hand it out

Every state decides by law or by an allocating agency how its cap is split. Some reserve a fixed share for multifamily housing; others take applications for all uses together. Many hold lotteries, rank applications or run rounds through the year.

Unused cap doesn't vanish right away

A state that doesn't use all its cap in a year can elect to carry it forward for certain purposes, including qualified rental housing, for up to three years.

Pick your state

title: Winning the award
blurb: How states score applications, who's on the team, and how to read the results.

lessons.title: What every state has to reward
lessons.body:
Every state writes its own scoring plan, the Qualified Allocation Plan (QAP). But federal law sets the floor. Every QAP must give preference to:

  • Projects serving the lowest-income residents.
  • Projects that stay affordable the longest.
  • Projects in qualified census tracts that contribute to a concerted community revitalization plan.

It also has to weigh a required list of criteria: location, housing needs, the project and sponsor, tenant populations with special needs, public housing waitlists, families with children, projects intended for eventual tenant ownership, energy efficiency, and historic buildings.

And it has to keep watching after the award, with compliance monitoring, regular site visits, and reporting problems it finds to the IRS.

Everything else, the points, weights, set-asides and tiebreakers, is up to the state. That's why every QAP reads so differently, and why developers re-read them every year.

Key points
  • Three required preferences.
  • A required list of criteria to weigh.
  • Ongoing monitoring.
  • Points and tiebreakers are up to each state.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(m)(1)(B)–(C).
26 U.S.C. § 42(m)(1)(A) (QAP approved after a public hearing under rules like § 147(f)(2); local notice; market study; written explanation for exceptions).
26 U.S.C. § 42(m)(2) (credit limited to the amount needed for feasibility; checked at application, allocation and placed in service).
IRS Rev. Rul. 2016-29 (local notice rule does not require or encourage local approval).
State scoring categories and the sample point split are general and made up for illustration; see each state’s QAP.
lessons.more:
How the plan itself gets made

A QAP isn't just an agency policy. Federal law says it has to be approved by an elected official of the state, usually the governor, after a public hearing. Most states put out a draft, take public comment, hold the hearing and adopt a new plan every year or two. Developers read every draft, because a one-point change can decide who wins.

Four federal rules tied to every award

  • Local notice. The agency has to tell the top elected official where the project would go, such as the mayor or county executive, and give them a reasonable chance to comment. The IRS has said this does not require, or encourage, letting a local government veto a deal.
  • A market study. An independent study of local housing need, paid for by the developer, has to come before the award. See the market study.
  • No more credit than needed. The agency can only award the amount of credit the deal needs to be financially feasible and viable for the long term. It checks this when the application comes in, when credits are awarded, and again when the building is placed in service.
  • A written reason for exceptions. If the agency awards credits outside its own priorities and scoring, it has to explain why in writing, and make that explanation public.

What states add on top

Past the federal floor, each state builds its own point system. Categories that show up in many QAPs:

  • Location: nearness to groceries, schools, transit, jobs or health care.
  • Deeper targeting: extra points for units set aside at lower incomes, or for longer affordability.
  • Cost and efficiency: limits on cost per unit, or points for asking for fewer credits.
  • Readiness: zoning in place, site control, financing commitments.
  • Experience: a track record of finishing and running deals.
  • Resident services, green building and local support.
Example, made-up numbers: a QAP with 100 possible points might give 20 for location, 15 each for income targeting, readiness and cost efficiency, 10 each for experience, resident services and local support, and 5 for green building. Real plans differ by state and change from year to year.

Tiebreakers

Because scores bunch up near the top, every QAP spells out how to break a tie. Each state picks its own, such as fewer credits per unit, distance to an amenity, or a set order of preferences. Read them as closely as the points.

Find your state's plan

lessons.title: The team it takes to build one deal
lessons.body:
One tax credit deal takes a lot of people. The core seats:

  • Developer: finds the site, runs the application, guarantees the deal.
  • Architect and engineers: design to code, to the QAP and to accessibility rules.
  • General contractor: prices and builds it.
  • Syndicator or investor: puts in equity in exchange for the credits.
  • Lenders: a construction loan and a permanent loan, sometimes the same bank.
  • Attorneys: usually several, for the developer, investor, lender and bonds.
  • Market analyst: proves there's demand.
  • Property manager: leases it up and keeps it in compliance for decades.

Add a CPA for the cost certification, often a tax credit consultant, and on public housing deals, the housing authority. The investor, the lenders and the state all have to approve before closing.

Key points
  • At least eight core seats.
  • Several attorneys, not one.
  • The property manager matters for 30+ years.
  • Investor, lenders and the state all approve before closing.
sources: General industry practice; roles, timing and guarantees vary by deal.
24 CFR Parts 50 and 58 (environmental review when HUD funds are used).
Predevelopment dollar amount is made up for illustration.
lessons.more:
Who's working when

StageWho's busy
Finding a siteDeveloper, land seller or broker, often an early look from a market analyst
ApplicationArchitect, civil engineer, market analyst, environmental consultant, tax credit consultant, attorney
Award to closingInvestor or syndicator, lenders, attorneys for every party, contractor finalizing price, title company, appraiser
ConstructionContractor, architect on site visits, the lender's and investor's construction inspectors
Lease-upProperty manager and its compliance staff
Cost certificationCPA, then the state issues IRS Form 8609
The next 15 to 30+ yearsProperty manager, the investor's asset manager, the state's compliance monitors

The third-party reports

Before an application or a closing, outside firms produce a stack of reports. Common ones:

  • Phase I environmental site assessment: checks for contamination.
  • Market study: proves demand at the planned rents.
  • Appraisal: values the land and the finished property.
  • Survey and soils report: boundaries, easements and what the ground can hold.
  • Capital needs assessment: for rehab deals, what needs fixing and when.
  • Federal environmental review: required when HUD money, such as HOME funds or project-based vouchers, is in the deal.

Who guarantees what

The investor is putting in millions and wants someone on the hook if things go wrong. That's usually the developer and its parent company. Common guarantees to the investor:

  • Construction completion: the building gets finished, even if it costs more.
  • Operating deficits: the developer covers shortfalls in the early years, usually up to a cap and for a set period.
  • Credit delivery: if fewer credits come through than promised, the investor gets money back.

That's why investors look hard at a developer's net worth and cash, not just its track record.

Who pays before the award

Example, made-up numbers: a developer spends $250,000 on site control, reports, design and fees to put in an application. If the deal wins, most of that gets paid back from the development budget at closing. If it loses, the developer usually eats it, or tries again next round.

lessons.title: The market study
lessons.body:
Before a state can award credits, federal law requires a comprehensive market study of the housing needs of low-income people in the area. It's done by a disinterested third party approved by the state, and the developer pays for it.

The study answers one question: will people rent these apartments at these rents? Things it looks at:

  • Capture rate: the share of qualified, income-eligible renters the project needs to fill. Lower is safer.
  • Absorption: how many months to lease up.
  • Rent advantage: how far the capped rents sit below comparable market rents.
  • Competition: other affordable properties nearby, open or in the pipeline.

States set their own thresholds, and many follow national market study standards. A weak study can sink an application before scoring even starts.

Key points
  • Required by federal law before an award.
  • Third party, paid for by the developer.
  • Capture rate, absorption and rent advantage.
  • States set the pass/fail lines.
sources: Metric definitions vary by state; see each state's QAP and market study guide.

lessons.title: How to read an award list
lessons.body:
Every state posts who applied and who won. It's public, and it's one of the best ways to learn the business.

  1. Find the list. Search your state housing finance agency's site for "housing tax credit awards" or "application log."
  2. Check the set-aside or region. Most states award by region and by pool (nonprofit, rural, elderly, at-risk). Applications only compete inside their pool.
  3. Look at the scores. Winners are often separated by a point or two, and ties are broken by rules written in the QAP.
  4. Divide credits by units. Annual credits per unit shows how much each deal needed, and how far over the state's limits it was pushing.
  5. Watch the waitlist. Returned credits go to the next deal in line, sometimes months later.
Key points
  • Award lists are public.
  • Deals compete within regions and pools.
  • Scores are often one or two points apart.
  • Credits per unit is the quickest comparison.
sources: State housing finance agency award and application logs; formats vary by state.

title: Paying for it
blurb: Who owns the deal, what it costs, why the loan is small, and how the gap gets filled.

lessons.title: Who actually owns a tax credit deal
lessons.body:
Developers win the credits. Then almost all of them go to someone else.

Each property is usually owned by its own partnership or LLC, set up just for that deal. The investor comes in as the limited partner and typically owns 99% to 99.99% of it. That's how it receives the credits and tax losses.

An affiliate of the developer is usually the general partner. It owns a tiny share, as little as 0.01%, but it runs the deal and carries the guarantees.

So how do developers get paid? Mostly through the developer fee, plus a negotiated share of cash flow and the eventual sale. As limited partners, investors generally can't lose more than they put in.

Key points
  • One partnership per deal.
  • Investor: 99% to 99.99%.
  • Developer side: a sliver, but runs it.
  • Developers earn fees.
sources: Kutak Rock, "Introduction to Tax Credits" (CDFA).
ABA Journal of Affordable Housing & Community Development Law.
Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(4)(ii) (partnership credits allocated in the same proportion as the related expenditures, such as depreciation).
26 U.S.C. § 469 (passive activity limits on individuals), § 42(i)(7) (right of first refusal after the compliance period).
12 CFR Parts 25, 228 and 345 (Community Reinvestment Act rules for banks).
General description only; ownership shares, fees and cash flow splits are made up or general and vary by deal.
lessons.more:
Example: where the credits go

Example, made-up numbers: a deal earns $1,000,000 of credits a year. The investor owns 99.99% of the partnership, so it gets $999,900 of credits a year, about $9,999,000 over 10 years. The developer's general partner, at 0.01%, gets $100 a year. The credits aren't why the developer is there.

The usual cast

SeatWho it usually isTypical shareWhat it does
OwnerA partnership or LLC set up for one property—Owns the land and building, signs the loans and the state agreement
General partner (or managing member)An affiliate of the developer, sometimes with a nonprofit partner0.01% or soRuns the property, hires the manager, gives guarantees
Investor limited partnerA fund put together by a syndicator, or one investor directly99% to 99.99%Puts in the equity, takes the credits and tax losses
Special limited partnerOften an affiliate of the syndicatorA tiny shareWatches over the investor's interests and can step in if the GP fails

Shares in the table are general ranges, not rules. Every partnership agreement is negotiated.

Why a partnership

The credit goes to whoever owns the building for tax purposes. A partnership passes its credits and losses through to its partners, so the investor can buy into the owner and use the credits on its own tax return. Tax rules generally require the credits to be split the same way as the related depreciation, which is why the investor holds almost all of both.

Most investors are corporations, often banks and insurance companies. Banks can also get Community Reinvestment Act consideration for these investments. Individuals can invest too, but passive activity rules limit how much of the credit most people can use.

Who gets the cash

Example, made-up numbers: after paying operating costs, the mortgage and reserve deposits, a property has $100,000 of cash flow in a year. Under one made-up agreement:
1. $5,000 annual fee to the investor side for asset management.
2. $60,000 toward the deferred developer fee.
3. The last $35,000 split 90% to the general partner and 10% to the investor.

Splits vary a lot. The investor's return mostly comes from the credits and tax losses, not the cash flow, which is why it can accept a small slice.

How it ends

After the 15-year compliance period, the investor usually wants out. The general partner often buys the investor's interest under terms set at the start. Or a nonprofit, tenant group or government agency holding a right of first refusal may buy the property itself. The affordability rules stay with the property. See Year 15.

Common myths

  • "The developer owns the building." The partnership does. The developer controls it through the general partner.
  • "The investor is buying a building." It's mostly buying tax credits and tax losses.
  • "Investors can lose more than they put in." As limited partners, generally not. The general partner carries the guarantees.

lessons.title: The six buckets in every development budget
lessons.body:
The capital stack is where the money comes from. The development budget is where it goes. Almost every budget sorts into six buckets:

  1. Acquisition: land, plus any existing buildings.
  2. Hard costs: construction, site work and a contingency.
  3. Soft costs: architecture, engineering, legal, the market study, permits, insurance, application fees.
  4. Financing costs: construction interest and loan and bond fees.
  5. Developer fee: capped by the state.
  6. Reserves: operating, replacement and lease-up reserves the investor and lender require.
Example, made-up numbers: a $20M budget might be $1M acquisition, $14M hard costs, $1.5M soft costs, $1M financing, $2M developer fee and $0.5M reserves.

Most of buckets 2 through 5 lands in eligible basis. Land and reserves don't. See what counts in basis.

Key points
  • Acquisition, hard, soft, financing, fee, reserves.
  • Hard costs are the biggest bucket.
  • Not every bucket earns credits.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(d) (eligible basis), § 42(m)(2)(A)–(B) (credit limited to the amount needed; reasonableness of development and operating costs).
26 U.S.C. § 147(g) (issuance costs paid from bond proceeds limited to 2% of proceeds).
GAO-18-637, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit: Improved Data and Oversight Would Strengthen Cost Assessment and Fraud Risk Management (2018).
Example numbers are made up for illustration. Cost caps, fee limits and reserve rules vary by state, lender and investor.
lessons.more:
Example: sources have to equal uses

The same made-up $20 million budget, with where the money comes from:

Uses (made-up)AmountSources (made-up)Amount
Acquisition$1,000,000Tax credit equity$13,000,000
Hard costs$14,000,000First mortgage$4,000,000
Soft costs$1,500,000Soft loan from a city or state$2,000,000
Financing costs$1,000,000Deferred developer fee$1,000,000
Developer fee$2,000,000
Reserves$500,000
Total$20,000,000Total$20,000,000

The two columns have to match. If costs go up and nothing else changes, the developer usually defers more of its fee, looks for more soft money, or cuts cost. See the capital stack lesson.

What's inside each bucket

  • Acquisition: the land price, closing costs, and for rehab deals, the existing buildings.
  • Hard costs: the building and site work, the contractor's general requirements, overhead and profit, and a construction contingency. Contingencies are commonly higher on rehab, where surprises hide in the walls. Many states cap the contractor's fees.
  • Soft costs: architecture, engineering, surveys, environmental reports, the market study, appraisal, legal, accounting, permits and impact fees, insurance during construction, and the state's application and monitoring fees.
  • Financing costs: construction loan interest and fees, permanent loan fees, and on bond deals, the cost of issuing the bonds. Federal law limits how much of that cost can be paid from the bond proceeds to 2% of the proceeds.
  • Developer fee: what the developer earns for the risk and work. States cap it, often as a percentage of costs, and part of it is often deferred and paid from cash flow.
  • Reserves: money set aside at closing, such as an operating reserve for bad years, a replacement reserve for roofs and appliances, and a lease-up reserve.

Which buckets earn credits

BucketIn eligible basis?
LandNo
Existing building (rehab deals)Yes, if it meets the acquisition rules
Hard costsMostly yes
Soft costsMostly yes
Construction loan interest and feesMostly yes
Permanent loan fees and syndication costsNo
Developer feeMostly yes
ReservesNo

The line-by-line answer depends on tax rules and the accountant's cost certification. See what counts in basis.

How it works in practice

The budget gets built at least three times: a rough version to pick the site, a detailed version for the state application, and a final version at closing with real bids. The state checks it each time, because federal law says it can only award as much credit as the deal needs, considering whether the development and operating costs are reasonable. Many states also set limits on total cost per unit. After construction, an accountant certifies what was actually spent.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the contingency as extra money. It's for real surprises, and leftover contingency may shrink basis at the end.
  • Forgetting reserves. Investors and lenders require them, and they don't earn credits.
  • Counting the deferred fee as paid. It's a cost in the budget, but the developer only gets it if the property produces cash flow.

lessons.title: Why the bank lends so little
lessons.body:
On a market-rate deal, the mortgage is often the biggest piece of the stack. On a tax credit deal, it's usually small. The reason is capped rents.

Lenders size a loan off net operating income (NOI) and a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), commonly 1.15 to 1.25. Capped rents mean capped NOI, which means a capped loan.

Example, made-up numbers: 60 units at an average rent of $900 is $648,000 a year. Less 7% vacancy leaves $602,640. Less operating costs of $5,500 a unit ($330,000) leaves NOI of $272,640. At a 1.20 DSCR, the deal can carry $227,200 a year of debt service. At 6.5% over 35 years, that supports a loan of about $3.1 million, on a deal that might cost $20 million.

That's why the rest has to come from equity and soft money, and why higher interest rates hit affordable deals so hard.

Key points
  • Loans are sized off NOI and DSCR.
  • Capped rents cap the loan.
  • Often 15% to 25% of the stack.
  • Rate increases shrink it further.
sources: Example numbers are made up; loan math is standard amortization at the rate and term shown.

lessons.title: The four most common soft-money sources
lessons.body:
Soft money is the cheap or forgivable layer that closes the gap. The four you'll see most:

  • HOME: HUD block grants to states and cities, created in 1990, used for loans or grants to affordable housing.
  • CDBG: Community Development Block Grants, a broader HUD program cities sometimes use for site work or infrastructure.
  • National Housing Trust Fund: created in 2008 and funded by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, aimed mostly at extremely low-income households.
  • FHLB Affordable Housing Program (AHP): each Federal Home Loan Bank sets aside at least 10% of its prior year's net income for competitive grants, applied for through a member bank.

Plus state and local trust funds, and sometimes the housing authority. Every source brings its own rules: income targeting, affordability periods, and with federal money, extra requirements like accessibility (Section 504) and, in some cases, Davis-Bacon wages. Funding levels change every year.

Key points
  • HOME, CDBG, Housing Trust Fund, FHLB AHP.
  • Cheap or forgivable, but competitive and slow.
  • Federal grants can reduce eligible basis, so many are made as loans.
  • Each source adds its own rules.
sources: HOME: Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act of 1990; 24 CFR Part 92.
National Housing Trust Fund: Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008; 24 CFR Part 93.
FHLB AHP: 12 U.S.C. § 1430(j); 12 CFR Part 1291.
CDBG: Housing and Community Development Act of 1974.

lessons.title: How the equity actually gets paid in
lessons.body:
The investor doesn't write one check at closing. Equity comes in installments, each tied to a milestone that lowers the investor's risk:

  1. Closing.
  2. Construction completion.
  3. Placed in service and lease-up.
  4. Stabilization or conversion to the permanent loan.
  5. Final cost certification and IRS Form 8609s.
Example, made-up numbers: $8.3M of equity paid 20% at closing, 40% at completion, 30% at stabilization and 10% at 8609s.

Because most equity arrives after construction, a construction loan bridges the gap. Some investors pay more up front for a lower price; others pay later for a higher one. That timing is part of every pricing negotiation.

Key points
  • Equity comes in milestones, not one check.
  • A construction loan bridges the timing.
  • Up-front vs. later pay-in affects price.
  • The last piece often waits on the 8609s.
sources: General industry practice; schedules are negotiated deal by deal.
IRS Form 8609, Low-Income Housing Credit Allocation and Certification.

lessons.title: The developer fee, and why part of it waits
lessons.body:
The developer fee pays the developer for the time, risk and guarantees it takes to get a deal built. States cap it in the QAP, often around 15% of development costs, though the formula varies a lot by state.

Most of the fee is in eligible basis, so it earns credits. But it's rarely all paid in cash. Part of it is usually deferred: left in the deal as a source of funds and paid later out of cash flow.

Investors generally want the deferred piece to be realistically paid off within about 15 years. If it can't be, the IRS could question whether it belongs in basis, which would shrink the credits.

So a deferred fee is the developer betting its own pay on the property performing.

Key points
  • Capped by each state.
  • Mostly in eligible basis.
  • Part is deferred and paid from cash flow.
  • It has to be realistically payable.
sources: State QAP developer fee limits (vary by state).
General tax practice on deferred developer fees; specifics depend on tax counsel.

lessons.title: Why construction costs sink deals
lessons.body:
On a market-rate deal, higher costs can be passed on through higher rents. On a tax credit deal, they can't. Rents are capped by the income limits.

Higher costs do raise eligible basis, and so the credit amount. But states cap how much credit one deal can get, and many cap cost per unit. Once a deal hits those limits, every extra dollar of cost is a dollar of gap.

That gap has to come from somewhere: more soft money, more deferred fee, a value-engineered design, or fewer units. If none of those works, the deal dies, sometimes after the award.

A federal review found per-unit costs vary widely from state to state, and that states use very different cost controls.

Key points
  • Rents are capped, so costs can't be passed on.
  • Credit and cost caps limit how far basis helps.
  • Extra cost becomes gap.
  • Gaps kill deals, even after an award.
sources: GAO-18-637, "Low-Income Housing Tax Credit: Improved Data and Oversight Would Strengthen Cost Assessment and Fraud Risk Management" (2018).
State QAP credit and cost limits (vary by state).

title: Living there
blurb: For renters: vouchers, utility allowances, raises, rent changes, senior housing and accessibility.

lessons.title: They can't turn you down for having a voucher
lessons.body:
Plenty of landlords turn down Section 8 vouchers. Tax credit properties can't do that just because you have one.

Every tax credit property awarded credits since 1990 signs a long-term agreement with the state. Federal law requires it to prohibit refusing a renter because they hold a Section 8 voucher. It lasts as long as the affordability rules do: at least 30 years.

It's not a free pass. You still have to income-qualify and meet the same screening rules as every other applicant.

The two programs fit together: the tax credit caps the rent on the apartment, and the voucher helps the renter pay it. To find properties near you, search for HUD's LIHTC database.

Key points
  • It's in every long-term agreement.
  • No refusing just for a voucher.
  • You still have to income-qualify.
  • Lasts 30+ years.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(6)(B)(iv) (extended use agreement must prohibit refusing to lease to a voucher holder because of that status).
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(6)(E)(ii) (three years of protection after the extended use period ends early).
26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(2)(B)(i) (Section 8 payments are not part of gross rent).
IRS, Guide for Completing Form 8823, ch. 7 (voucher rule applies to allocations from 1990 on; annual owner certification) and ch. 11 (Section 8 tenants and the gross rent limit).
24 CFR § 982.507 (rent reasonableness), § 982.508 (family share at move-in no more than 40% of adjusted income).
HUD LIHTC Database (huduser.gov).
Example rents are made up. State and local source-of-income laws vary; not legal advice.
lessons.more:
The rule in plain English

Every tax credit property has a long-term agreement with the state, often called the extended use agreement or LURA. Federal law says that agreement has to prohibit refusing to rent to someone because they hold a Section 8 voucher. It covers properties awarded credits from 1990 on. The owner certifies every year that it's following the agreement, and the state's compliance staff check.

Example: how the rent works with a voucher

Example, made-up numbers: a two-bedroom's tax credit maximum gross rent is $1,100, and the utility allowance is $100. Without a voucher, the most a renter can be charged is $1,000.
With a voucher, the housing authority might approve a rent of $1,150. The voucher pays part, and the renter pays the rest. Because a Section 8 payment is coming in, the total rent can be above the tax credit cap. The renter's share is set by the voucher program, usually around 30% of adjusted income. At move-in, if the rent is above the housing authority's payment standard, the renter's share, including utilities, can't be more than 40% of adjusted income.

The tax credit cap only limits what renters pay themselves. Without a voucher or other rent help, the rent can't go over the cap.

What the rule does and doesn't do

  • It does stop a property from saying "we don't take vouchers," or from turning someone down for that reason.
  • It doesn't create an open apartment. If the property is full or has a waitlist, voucher holders wait like everyone else.
  • It doesn't skip income rules. Voucher holders still have to income-qualify for the tax credit unit.
  • It doesn't skip screening. Renters meet the same written screening rules as other applicants, and those rules have to follow fair housing law.
  • The voucher has its own steps. The housing authority has to approve the rent as reasonable, and the unit has to pass its inspection before the voucher pays.

How long it lasts

The rule runs as long as the agreement: at least 30 years, and longer in many states. The usual Year 15 investor exit doesn't end it. Even if the agreement does end early, through foreclosure or the "qualified contract" process (the owner asks the state to find a buyer and none is found), existing low-income renters get three more years of protection: no eviction without good cause, and no rent increases beyond what the tax credit rules allow.

Common myths

  • "Every landlord has to take vouchers." Not under this rule. It covers tax credit properties. Some states and cities have their own source-of-income laws that reach further.
  • "The property is full, so it's refusing my voucher." A real waitlist isn't a refusal.
  • "With a voucher I can rent any size unit." The housing authority sets the voucher's bedroom size.

If you think you were turned down for having a voucher

Write down the date, the property and what was said. The state agency that monitors the property can look into it, and so can a local fair housing group or HUD's fair housing office. The renter page has links. This is general information, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Why your rent is lower than the cap
lessons.body:
The rent cap on a tax credit apartment is a gross rent cap. It includes an allowance for any utilities you pay yourself, like electricity or gas. (Phone, cable and internet don't count.)

Example, made-up numbers: if the maximum gross rent is $1,200 and the utility allowance is $150, the most you can be charged in rent is $1,050.

Where the allowance comes from depends on the building. Properties with Rural Development or HUD project-based assistance use those agencies' figures. Others can use the local housing authority's schedule, or an estimate from the utility company, the state agency, HUD's utility model or an energy consumption model.

Allowances are reviewed at least once a year. A change usually takes effect after a 90-day notice period.

Key points
  • Rent cap includes utilities you pay.
  • Allowance = cap minus what you can be charged.
  • Source depends on the building.
  • Reviewed at least yearly.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(2)(B)(ii) (gross rent includes the utility allowance).

Treas. Reg. § 1.42-10(a) (phone, cable TV and internet excluded), (b) (which allowance applies; HUD-assisted tenants use the housing authority allowance), (c)(1) (new allowance used for rents due 90 days after a change), (c)(2) (annual review), (e) (submetering).
IRS, Guide for Completing Form 8823, ch. 18 (utility allowances).
HUD FY2026 Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project income limits (huduser.gov), via the county lookup. Estimate, not a primary source.
Example rents and allowances are made up.
lessons.more:
Example: same building, different rents

Three two-bedroom apartments in one building, all with a $1,200 maximum gross rent (made-up numbers):

Who pays which utilitiesUtility allowanceMost you can be charged
Owner pays everything$0$1,200
You pay electric only$90$1,110
You pay electric, gas and water$180$1,020

The more utilities you pay yourself, the lower the rent cap on what you pay the landlord.

Look up the maximum gross rents by county

Subtract your building's utility allowance from the gross rent for your unit's income level and size. That's roughly the most the rent can be. The property manager has the exact numbers.

Which allowance applies

  • Rural Development buildings, or any building where a tenant gets Rural Development rental assistance: the Rural Development allowance.
  • HUD-regulated buildings, where HUD sets the rents and allowances: HUD's allowance.
  • Everyone else: units where the renter gets HUD rental assistance, such as a voucher, use the local public housing authority's allowance. For other units, the housing authority's allowance is the default, and the owner can instead use a written estimate from the utility company, an estimate from the state agency if it offers one, HUD's Utility Schedule Model, or an energy consumption model done by a licensed engineer or other qualified professional who isn't related to the owner.

How changes work

  • The owner has to review the allowance at least once each calendar year.
  • When an allowance changes, the new one has to be used for rents due 90 days after the change. If it goes up, the most you can be charged goes down.
  • Most owner-chosen estimates have to go to the state agency and be made available to tenants before that 90-day period starts.

Submeters

Some buildings buy utilities in bulk and bill each apartment through its own meter. If the bill reflects your actual use and the rate is no higher than the owner pays, it's treated as a utility you pay yourself, so it gets an allowance too. Any billing fee has to be figured the same way for every unit, and it's capped, generally at $5 a month unless a higher limit applies.

Common myths

  • "The rent cap is what I'll pay." The cap is gross rent: rent plus the allowance for utilities you pay.
  • "My rent should change with my utility bill." No. The allowance is an estimate for the building, not your actual bill.
  • "Internet counts as a utility." No. Phone, cable TV and internet don't count.

Questions you can ask the manager

  • Which utilities do I pay, and what's the allowance for my unit size?
  • Where does the allowance come from, and when was it last updated?
  • What's the maximum gross rent for my unit's income level?

lessons.title: Income averaging in four rules
lessons.body:
Income averaging, added to the law in 2018, lets one building serve a wider range of incomes.

  1. At least 40% of units must be rent-restricted and occupied by households that qualify at each unit's level (25% in New York City).
  2. Each restricted unit gets a designated income limit in 10% steps, from 20% to 80% of AMI.
  3. The designations must average 60% of AMI or less.
  4. Each unit's rent is capped based on its own designated limit.
Example, made-up numbers: a 100-unit building designates 20 units at 30% AMI, 40 at 60% and 40 at 80%. The average is 62%, which fails. Move 10 of the 80% units down to 60%, and the average is exactly 60%, which works.

The appeal: deeply affordable units for very low-income families and workforce units in the same building, with the higher rents helping carry the lower ones.

Key points
  • 40% minimum.
  • Limits from 20% to 80% in 10% steps.
  • Average must be 60% or less.
  • Rent follows each unit's limit.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(1)(C) (average income test, added by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018).
26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(2)(D)(iii)–(v) (140% next-available-unit rule for income averaging buildings).
26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(1) (the set-aside election is irrevocable), § 42(g)(2)(C) (rents figured on 1.5 people per bedroom).
Treas. Reg. § 1.42-19 and § 1.42-15(c), T.D. 9967 (final rules, Oct. 12, 2022: qualified groups of units, designations, limited changes, annual reporting).
HUD FY2026 Multifamily Tax Subsidy Project income limits (huduser.gov), via the county lookup. Estimate, not a primary source.
Example limits and rents are made up.
lessons.more:
Example: the rent at each level

Example, made-up numbers: in one county, the income limit for a three-person household at 60% of AMI is $60,000. A two-bedroom's rent is figured on three people (1.5 per bedroom). Each level's limit is a share of that, and the maximum gross rent is 30% of the limit, divided by 12.
Unit's designated levelIncome limit (3 people)Max gross rent, 2BR
30% of AMI$30,000$750
60% of AMI$60,000$1,500
80% of AMI$80,000$2,000

The rent cap includes the utility allowance. See why your rent is lower than the cap.

Look up limits and rents by county

The rules in plain English

  • It's a choice, made once. Income averaging is one of three minimum set-asides. The owner picks it for the project, and the choice can't be undone.
  • The units are averaged, not the people. Each unit gets a designated level. The test averages those levels, one unit, one vote.
  • Designations get recorded. The owner records each unit's level in its books and reports the designations to the state every year.
  • One problem unit doesn't sink the project. Under the 2022 final rules, the project passes as long as some group of at least 40% of its units qualifies and averages 60% or less. A unit outside that group can still lose credits for its own building.
  • Levels are mostly fixed. An owner can change a unit's level only in limited cases, such as a qualified tenant moving to another unit or fixing the average.

If your income goes up

Your unit stays affordable and your rent stays capped at your unit's level.
