If your income goes above 140% of the greater of 60% of AMI or your unit's level, the owner has to rent the next comparable or smaller vacant unit in the building to a household at the income level needed to keep the designations averaging 60% or less. See what happens if you get a raise.

Common myths

  • "Every unit is a 60% unit." Not in an income averaging building. Neighbors may have different limits and rents.
  • "80% units are market rate." No. They're still income-restricted and rent-capped, just at a higher level.
  • "My income gets averaged with my neighbors'." No. You qualify against your own unit's limit.

Questions you can ask the manager

  • What income level is this unit designated at?
  • What's the income limit and maximum rent at that level for my household size?

lessons.title: What happens if you get a raise
lessons.body:
A common worry: if I earn more, does my rent go up or do I have to move? Usually, neither.

You have to qualify when you move in. After that, a raise doesn't kick you out. Your rent stays capped by the unit's limit, not your paycheck.

The one rule that kicks in is the 140% rule. If your household income rises above 140% of the current income limit, your unit still counts as affordable. But the owner must rent the next available unit of comparable or smaller size to a qualified household.

In buildings where every unit is affordable, federal law doesn't require yearly income checks after move-in, though many states still require them.

Key points
  • Qualify at move-in.
  • A raise doesn't change your rent cap.
  • Over 140%: the next available unit goes to a qualified renter.
  • Some states still require yearly income checks.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(8)(B) (recertification for 100% low-income buildings).
Not legal advice; property and state rules vary.

lessons.title: When rents can go up
lessons.body:
Yes, rents at tax credit properties can go up. Here's how.

Every year, HUD publishes new income limits for tax credit properties. For fiscal 2026 they took effect May 1, 2026, and properties had a 45-day grace period to start using them. When the limits rise, the maximum rents rise too.

There are guardrails. HUD capped the increase at 10% for fiscal 2026, and the average change across areas was about 3.4%. A federal hold-harmless rule keeps a project's limits from falling below the highest level it has reached.

Owners aren't required to charge the maximum. Lease terms, notice rules and other funding sources can also limit increases. The utility allowance can change too, which moves the rent in the other direction.

Key points
  • Limits are updated every year by HUD.
  • Higher limits mean higher maximum rents.
  • FY2026 increases were capped at 10%.
  • Owners don't have to charge the max.
sources: HUD, FY2026 Income Limits and MTSP Income Limits (huduser.gov).
National Law Review, "HUD Releases 2026 Income Limits" (2026) (10% cap, 3.4% average).
Minnesota Housing, FY2026 limits bulletin (45-day grace period).
Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, § 3009 (hold harmless).
lessons.more: See your county's current limits

lessons.title: Senior vs. family deals
lessons.body:
Many tax credit properties are age-restricted. Under fair housing law, there are two ways to do it:

  • 62 and older: every resident is 62+.
  • 55 and older: at least 80% of occupied units have at least one resident who's 55+, and the property follows policies showing it's meant for older adults.

They pencil differently than family deals. Senior deals are mostly one-bedrooms, so rent per unit is lower. They usually need elevators, more common space and more accessible units. Some states reserve credits or points specifically for elderly housing.

Family deals have more two- and three-bedroom units and higher rents per unit, but more wear, more turnover and different amenities, like playgrounds.

Key points
  • Two legal options: 62+ or 55+.
  • Senior deals skew to one-bedrooms.
  • Elevators and common space add cost.
  • Some QAPs set aside credits for seniors.
sources: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b), as amended by the Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995.
24 CFR Part 100, Subpart E.

lessons.title: The accessibility rules every new deal meets
lessons.body:
Several layers of law apply, and a tax credit deal usually triggers more than one:

  • Fair Housing Act: for buildings with 4 or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991, every unit in an elevator building and every ground-floor unit otherwise must meet seven basic design requirements, like accessible routes, wider doors and reinforced bathroom walls.
  • Section 504: if the deal has federal financial assistance, like HOME or CDBG, at least 5% of units must be fully accessible for people with mobility disabilities and another 2% for people with hearing or vision disabilities.
  • ADA Title III: covers the leasing office and other areas open to the public.

On top of that, many state QAPs require or reward more accessible units. And for tax credit properties, a final fair housing discrimination finding is treated as noncompliance.

Key points
  • Fair Housing Act design rules apply to most new apartments.
  • Section 504 adds 5% mobility and 2% sensory units with federal funds.
  • ADA covers public areas.
  • States often require more.
sources: 24 CFR § 8.22 (Section 504).
28 CFR Part 36 (ADA Title III).
Treas. Reg. § 1.42-9 (general public use).

lessons.title: What supportive housing is
lessons.body:
Supportive housing is affordable housing paired with services, like case management, health care coordination or job help, for people who need them to stay housed. That often means people leaving homelessness, people with disabilities, or veterans.

The housing is usually financed with tax credits like any other deal. What's different:

  • Rental assistance is usually needed so residents with very low or no income can pay rent.
  • Services are funded separately, by sources like Medicaid, HUD homeless programs or state funds.
  • Service fees paid by a government program aren't counted as rent under the tax credit rules.

Many QAPs give points for supportive housing units. The hard part is that all three pieces, building, rental assistance and services, have to be lined up for decades.

Key points
  • Housing plus services.
  • Usually needs rental assistance.
  • Services are funded separately.
  • All three pieces have to last.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(g)(2)(B)(iii) (supportive service fees); § 42(i)(3)(B)(iii) (transitional housing for the homeless).

title: The long game
blurb: The deadlines after an award, what happens when rules get broken, Year 15, and rebuilding public housing.

lessons.title: You won. The clock started.
lessons.body:
Winning tax credits feels like the finish line. It's really the starting gun.

  • Before the award: a market study, paid for by the developer, done by an independent firm the state approves.
  • Within 12 months: if the building won't be finished in the award year, the owner's basis in the project has to be more than 10% of its expected total within a year of the allocation.
  • By the end of year 2: the building has to be placed in service by the end of the second calendar year after the award year.
Example, made-up numbers: award in June 2027. More than 10% of expected basis in place by June 2028. Placed in service by December 31, 2029.

The 10% test and the placed-in-service deadline apply to 9% allocations. 4% bond deals still need the market study, but they don't get an allocation from the state's credit ceiling, so the rest of their clock runs on bond and issuer timelines. Miss a deadline and the allocation fails; the credits go back to the state to hand out again. Closing the land, the loans and the investor, permits, and construction all have to fit inside that window.

Key points
  • Market study before the award.
  • More than 10% of basis within 12 months.
  • Placed in service by the end of year 2.
  • Miss it and the credits go back.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(m)(1)(A)(iii) (market study before allocation).
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(1)(E) (10% test one year after allocation; placed in service by the close of the second calendar year after the allocation year).
Treas. Reg. § 1.42-6 (carryover-allocation basis includes land; agency verification by owner, CPA or attorney certification).
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(3)(C) (returned credits go back to the state ceiling).
26 U.S.C. § 42(f)(1) (credit period), § 42(g)(3)(A) (set-aside met by end of first credit year), § 42(i)(1) (compliance period), § 42(l)(1) (Form 8609).
26 U.S.C. § 42(h)(4)(B) as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 (50% bond test; 25% when an issue dated after 2025 finances at least 5%).
IRS Rev. Proc. 2014-49 (relief, including deadline extensions, after major disasters).
Example dates, amounts and construction times are made up or general; every deal differs.
lessons.more:
The rules in plain English

  • Market study first. Before the state allocates credits, a comprehensive market study of local housing need has to be done by a disinterested party the agency approves, at the developer's expense. See the market study lesson.
  • The 10% test. A building placed in service in the award year doesn't need it. Every other 9% award does. One year after the allocation date, the owner's basis in the project has to be more than 10% of the basis it reasonably expects to have when the building is done. The state has to verify it, usually with a certification from the owner or from a CPA or attorney.
  • Placed in service by the end of year 2. Counted in calendar years, not months: an award any time in 2027 means a December 31, 2029 deadline.
  • After that, a new clock. The 10-year credit period starts the year the building is placed in service, or the next year if the owner elects. The minimum set-aside has to be met by the end of the first year of the credit period, and the 15-year compliance period starts with that first credit year.

Example: does the deal pass the 10% test?

Example, made-up numbers: the state signs a carryover allocation on October 15, 2027. The project's expected basis, land plus everything depreciable, is $20,000,000. By October 15, 2028 the owner needs more than $2,000,000 of basis.
Land closed: $1,500,000. Architecture, engineering and permits: $400,000. That's $1,900,000, short. Add $200,000 of early site work and fees paid, and the total is $2,100,000, which passes.

Land counts toward this test, even though land never counts in eligible basis and never earns credits. That's one reason many deals close on the land early.

Why the award date matters

Award date (made-up)10% test duePlaced-in-service deadlineTime to build
January 15, 2027January 15, 2028December 31, 2029About 35 months
December 15, 2027December 15, 2028December 31, 2029About 24 months

Same deadline, almost a year less time. A deal awarded late in the year has to close and start building fast.

How it works in practice

  1. Award and carryover. The state reserves the credits, then signs a carryover allocation agreement, usually by the end of the award year.
  2. Closing. Land, construction loan, permanent loan commitment, investor and any soft money all close, often 6 to 12 months after the award.
  3. Construction. Often 12 to 24 months, depending on size and type.
  4. Placed in service. For new construction, generally when the first unit is certified as ready to live in.
  5. Cost certification and Form 8609. An accountant certifies the final costs, and the state issues IRS Form 8609, which the owner needs to claim the credits.

4% bond deals run on a different clock

A 4% deal gets its credits from tax-exempt bonds instead of the state's 9% ceiling, so there's no carryover allocation and no 10% test. Its pressure points are the bond side: winning a share of the state's private activity bond cap, issuing the bonds before that award expires under state rules, and financing enough of the building with them. The bond test is 50% of the building and land, or 25% if bonds from an issue dated after 2025 finance at least 5% of the building and land. See the bond cap lesson.

Common mistakes

  • "12 months from the end of the year." No. The 10% test runs from the allocation date.
  • "Land doesn't count." It does for the 10% test, even though it doesn't for eligible basis.
  • "The 15 years start at the award." No. The compliance period starts with the first year of the credit period, after the building is placed in service.
  • "A missed deadline just means a late fee." A missed federal deadline means the allocation fails and the credits go back to the state. Some states have their own deadlines and return-and-reapply policies, but outside IRS disaster relief they can't extend the federal deadlines.

lessons.title: When a property breaks the rules
lessons.body:
Tax credit properties report to the state every year and get monitored, with file reviews of tenant income records and physical inspections.

When the state finds a problem, like an over-income tenant, an unsafe unit or rent over the cap, it tells the owner, who generally gets up to 90 days to fix it, extendable to six months. The state must then report it to the IRS on Form 8823, even if it was corrected.

Consequences during the 15-year compliance period:

  • Credits can be lost for any unit and year out of compliance.
  • If the building's qualified basis drops, part of the credits already claimed can be recaptured, with interest.

After year 15, the IRS steps back, and the state enforces the extended use agreement.

Key points
  • Annual reporting and state monitoring.
  • A correction period, then Form 8823 to the IRS.
  • Lost credits and recapture during years 1–15.
  • The state enforces years 16–30+.
sources: Treas. Reg. § 1.42-5.
IRS, Guide for Completing Form 8823.

lessons.title: Year 15: how the investor exits
lessons.body:
Once the 15-year compliance period ends, the investor has gotten its credits and usually wants out. Common paths:

  • Sale to the general partner: the developer side buys the investor's interest or the property, often under an option written into the partnership agreement.
  • Nonprofit right of first refusal: if the partnership agreement grants one, a qualified nonprofit, tenant group or government agency can buy at a minimum price, roughly the outstanding debt plus the investor's exit taxes.
  • Qualified contract: after year 14, an owner can ask the state to find a buyer at a formula price. If none is found within a year, the extended use period ends, though existing tenants keep protections for three more years. Many states now require owners to waive this option.

Year 15 is also when many properties get rehabbed with a new round of credits, called resyndication.

Key points
  • Investors usually exit after year 15.
  • The GP often buys them out.
  • Nonprofits can have a right of first refusal.
  • Many states require waiving the qualified contract.
sources: 26 U.S.C. § 42(i)(7) (right of first refusal), § 42(h)(6)(E)–(F), (I) (qualified contract).
Not legal advice; exits depend on each partnership agreement.

lessons.title: How old public housing gets rebuilt (RAD)
lessons.body:
Public housing nationwide has a big backlog of repairs, and the old funding model doesn't let housing authorities borrow against it. The Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD), created in 2012, fixes that.

RAD converts public housing units to long-term Section 8 contracts, either project-based vouchers or project-based rental assistance. With a steady contract, the property can take on debt and tax credit equity to renovate or rebuild.

Residents keep key protections, including the right to return after construction without being re-screened.

Scale: Congress capped conversions at 455,000 public housing units. As of October 2025, about 188,000 public housing units had converted, and in Maryland, Tennessee and Vermont more than half of the public housing that existed in 2012 has converted, according to HUD. Some deals blend RAD with Section 18, another tool for repositioning public housing. In May 2026, HUD began winding down Restore-Rebuild (formerly Faircloth-to-RAD), which had let authorities use RAD to build new units.

Key points
  • Converts public housing to Section 8 contracts.
  • Lets housing authorities borrow and use tax credits.
  • Residents have a right to return.
  • Capped at 455,000 units.
sources: HUD, RAD Overview (August 2026) (state-level conversion shares).
National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2026 Advocates' Guide, RAD chapter (188,493 units converted as of Oct. 1, 2025).
National Housing Law Project, RAD resources (455,000-unit cap).
Nelson Mullins and Nixon Peabody alerts, May 2026 (Restore-Rebuild wind-down).
